title: Can Folding Models Tell Binders from Bluffers? Evidence from POISK: The Patent-Derived Antibody Dataset
summary: Structure prediction models are increasingly deployed as zero-shot digital screens in antibody design, operating under the assumption that high folding confidence implies true binding. However, rigorous validation of this premise has been limited by small test sets, narrow target diversity, and the risk of data leakage from training-adjacent structures. Here we introduce POISK: Patent-extracted Organization of Immunoglobulin Sequence Knowledge, a large-scale dataset derived from the US patent literature, comprising 89074 antibody-antigen records extracted from 10110 patents using an LLM-based pipeline. From this resource, we curate a balanced benchmark set of 22494 complexes: 11247 patent-validated binders without a known resolved structure paired with putative non-binders constructed from sequence-similar human repertoire antibodies. Using this dataset, we benchmark six leading structure prediction models (AlphaFold-Multimer, Boltz-2, IntelliFold v2, OpenFold3, Protenix-v1, and Protenix-v2) on their ability to discriminate binders from decoys. The best-performing model, Protenix-v2, achieves 72% pairwise accuracy over all pairs and 87% on the most confident half of predictions, and correctly identifies the true binder from a pool of 50 candidates in 29% of trials; this represents a substantial enrichment over random selection, yet remains far from reliable single-candidate identification. Structural consensus across models also discriminates binders from decoys, with pairwise accuracy reaching 73.1% when three or more models converge on a pose (DockQ>0.23, covering around 54.2% of pairs). Epitope localization remains unreliable: the best model contacts annotated epitope residues in only 62.8% of cases, indicating that binding discrimination does not establish accurate epitope localization. Our results suggest that current folding models provide useful but limited signal for antibody screening and should be complemented by orthogonal methods. We release POISK as a community resource for future benchmarking and model training.

title: Computational Design and Evaluation of De Novo Protein Minibinders Targeting Specific Sites of STAT3
summary: STAT3 is a transcription factor involved in the progression of many types of cancer, which makes it an attractive therapeutic target. Small-molecule STAT3 inhibitors have experienced a high failure rate in clinical trials, indicating alternative approaches may be warranted. To address these limitations, we used BindCraft, a modern AI-driven protein design tool, to create miniprotein binder candidates against several sites of STAT3. We selected seven target hotspots on the SH2, linker, DNA-binding and coiled-coil domains of STAT3. Of 139 designs that passed BindCraft's filters, 11 high-confidence binders emerged from five of the seven hotspots. These candidate binders were evaluated with AlphaFold3 (AF3). All eleven are predicted to dock with their intended domain; most within 4.5 Å of one or more of their targeted hotspot residues. Several minibinders are predicted to dock simultaneously to STAT3 without overlap. Such pairs have the potential to constitute STAT3 sandwich assays. BLASTp searches found no matches with known protein sequences for six of the binders and only very low-significance matches for the other five. We disclose herein the sequences of our top binders targeting diverse regions of the STAT3 surface with the hope that experimental validation by the broader research community will yield promising leads for preclinical drug development against this important cellular regulator.

title: Function-preserving CD8⁺ T Cell Immunogenicity minimization through protein design
summary: Rapid advances in protein design enable new approaches in adoptive cell therapy, but foreign proteins can elicit cytotoxic T cell responses, and hence there is considerable need for approaches which reduce immunogenicity without compromising protein function. Here, we develop a computational framework integrating structure-guided sequence design with MHC class I epitope prediction to efficiently tune protein immunogenicity while preserving function. Using a de novo-designed luciferase as a model, we demonstrate epitope elimination while preserving function across 5 common mouse alleles and extend our computational optimization to 25 common human MHC-I alleles. In mice immunized with mRNA-lipid nanoparticles, variants designed to have few MHC-I epitopes elicited little detectable CD8⁺ T cell response, whereas variants designed to include multiple epitopes induced robust responses. Together, these results demonstrate that the CD8⁺ T cell immunogenicity of designed proteins can be tuned while preserving function, opening the door to incorporation of designed proteins in a next generation of adoptive cell therapies.

title: GLOM TGITO: multiscale protein modelling and multiview landscape-guided sequence discovery
summary: Motivation: Offline protein design can exploit surrogate-predictor errors, favouring high-scoring sequences lacking measured support. We test whether multiscale representations and local experimental evidence improve prediction and candidate prioritization. Results: GLOM-TGITO links a global-local fluorescence predictor to multiview landscape-guided optimization. Across 31,434 measured ppluGFP2 sequences, GLOM achieved random/depth-holdout RMSEs of 0.170/0.247 versus 0.247/0.324 for the strongest SaProt-650M controls. Averaged across three training seeds, 96.3%/97.3% of prediction-ranked Top 100 test variants were measured bright (log10 fluorescence >=4.2). Search from 900 peak regions yielded 2,594 distinct candidate sequences. The selected Top 100 showed 2.9-8.2% lower mean representation deviation than four comparator pipelines; 38 versus 11-16 met joint novelty-reliability filters.
